headline: Referred private-way snow removal ballot order to full Council; kept private-way upkeep funding resolution in committee.
summary: Councilors discussed private ways, which the City does not formally accept, and a state law that allows paying to plow them. Commissioner McGivern said the City already removes snow and ice on private ways as an emergency measure, and disputed claims that it has appropriated $0 for private way repairs.
decisions: Referred Order 26-172 to a future City Council meeting, with a request for legal counsel to clarify liability for snow removal on private ways; vote 5-0.
Kept Resolution 26-182 in committee, with requests for website information and legal guidance on a budget line item for private ways; vote 5-0.

decision_titles: Order 26-172 on Section 6C snow removal on private ways
Resolution 26-182 on private way routine maintenance and upkeep
plain_text:
1 
 
PUBLIC WORKS AND FACILITIES COMMITTEE  
MEETING REPORT 
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 @ 6:00pm 
 
Call to Order 
 
Chair Callahan called the meeting to order. Present were Chair Callahan, Councilor Leming, 
Councilor Scarpelli, Vice President Lazzaro, and President Bears. Councilor Tseng was also 
present. 
 
 
26-172 – Order to Place Adoption of M.G.L. chapter 40, Section 6C Before Voters in 
November 2027 (Regarding Liability on Private Ways) 
 
Resolution: 
 
Whereas, in Gallagher v. City of Medford, a resident brought suit against the City after suffering 
injuries caused by a defect on a private way; and, 
 
Whereas, the City sought summary judgment, arguing it had no maintenance obligation over 
private ways; and, 
 
Whereas, the Appellate Division of the District Court Department found that the City's informal 
maintenance on that private way — performed without the City having adopted M.G.L. c. 40 
§6C — estopped the City from denying that way's public status under G.L. c. 84, §25; and,  
 
Whereas, the Court stated directly: "It is undeniable that a city or town which has accepted G.L. 
c.40 §6C may remove snow and ice from a private way without risk that such services will 
constitute repairs cognizable under G.L. c.84, §25;" and, 
 
Whereas, following the *Gallagher* ruling, the City has not acted to adopt G.L. c. 40 §6C; and 
 
Whereas, the City of Medford continues to perform informal maintenance, sweeping, and snow 
and ice removal on all private ways; and 
 
Whereas, Section 6C's liability carve-out only protects the City if the City has actually accepted 
it; and 
 
Whereas, 39% of Medford roadways are designated private ways; and 
 
Whereas, since 2020, the City has appropriated $0.00 for private way repairs; and 
 
Whereas, no maintenance or upkeep services are provided but for the informal services outlined 
in Gallagher; and 
 
Whereas, without acceptance, the City is unnecessarily exposing itself to full public-way tort 
liability; and 
 
Whereas, acceptance of the measure requires a ballot question at the next regular City election; 
now, therefore:
2 
 
 
By the Medford City Council that we hereby vote, pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws 
Chapter 40, Section 6D, to submit for acceptance to the registered voters of the City, at the next 
regular City election, the question of whether the City shall accept the provisions of 
Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40, Section 6C. 
 
Discussion: 
 
Councilor Scarpelli emphasized that the intent of the resolution is to help clarify misconceptions 
and misunderstandings regarding private ways, and help residents understand what the City is 
doing, what it is able to do, and what residents’ responsibilities are. His focus is on establishing 
a line item that identifies for the City Council what is available for private ways. 
 
Chair Callahan invited Councilor Tseng to provide a summary of Mass General Laws Chapter 
40, Section 6. Councilor Tseng reviewed his presentation titled “Snow Removal on Private 
Ways M.G.L. c. §40 6C,” a copy of which is attached hereto. 
 
Councilor Leming expressed that, whether or not it succeeds, having a ballot question will serve 
as a public education initiative to make residents more aware of the private vs. public way 
distinction. If it passes, it would allow the City to make progress on the issue, and if it were to 
fail, voters would understand that at least the City tried to address the issue.  
 
Prior to the meeting, Commissioner of Public Works Tim McGivern sent an email to the Council 
addressing the topic of private ways, a copy of which is attached hereto. In the meeting, 
Commissioner McGivern thanked Councilor Tseng for his presentation. He clarified that Section 
6C would address only snow and ice removal on private ways. He believes that a ballot initiative 
would pass since the City already does remove snow and ice on private ways as an emergency 
measure. He also clarified that private ways are not always owned by the abutters , but that 
under the state’s Derelict Fee Statute, unless a deed specifies otherwise, ownership of and 
responsibility for a private way defaults to the abutters of the way. He stated that the City takes 
the position that the public has right of access on private ways, which includes dead-end private 
ways because public services still need the ability to access the end of the dead-end, and 
therefore property owners abutting a private way may not blockade the road.  
 
Commissioner McGivern stated that, if the City were to adopt Section 6C, it would limit liability 
for the City for removing snow and ice from private ways, similar to the City’s existing liability 
limits for snow and ice removal on public ways. 
 
Commissioner McGivern noted that the City has an existing ordinance under Chapter 40, 
Section 6N which allows a municipality to make temporary repairs to private ways, but 
highlighted that public obligations come first. The City owns and operates a public way network 
of roads, and all property owners pay taxes into that public way network regardless of whether 
they live on a private way or a public way. City taxes pay to upkeep. As a result, the City has not 
been making use of the ordinance because the City’s obligation for public road upkeep is so 
large. However, some funds are spent on private way repairs currently, and those repairs are 
included in the highway operation budget appropriated each year, although the amount 
expended on private ways is not tracked separately. 
 
With respect to trees on private ways, Commission McGivern explained that, while the paper 
being discussed was focused on the provisions of Section 6C for snow and ice removal on 
private Ways, unless a tree is publicly protected under Chapter 87 of Mass General Laws, the
3 
 
obligation to maintain a tree runs with the land and falls to the title holders of the land. However, 
the City does assist with trees on private ways in public emergency situations where a tree 
poses an immediate threat to the public. He acknowledged that the City has worked on trees on 
private properties in the past, and there has not always been clarity of what the Department of 
Public Works is and is not able to do, but they are working to clarify what the policies are. 
 
Addressing the Council: 
Paul Gerety 
Jean Diskin  
Sharon Deyeso  
 
Motion by President Bears to refer the matter to a future Regular Meeting of the City Council, 
as amended by Councilor Scarpelli to request legal counsel provide clarification on the liabilities 
for snow removal on private ways, seconded by Councilor Scarpelli. Approved on a Roll Call 
Vote of Five in favor, Zero opposed. 
 
 
26-182 - Resolution on Routine Maintenance and Upkeep of Private Ways 
 
Resolution: 
 
WHEREAS, Chapter 90 funds are state aid, restricted for use on public ways only; 
 
 
WHEREAS, on average Medford's annual Chapter 90 aid hovers around $990k; 
 
WHEREAS, the City Administration, in its annual budget since 2020, relies solely on Chapter 90 
funds for the maintenance and upkeep of City roads; 
 
WHEREAS, the City Administration has a policy of refusing to perform certain routine 
maintenance and upkeep of private ways, citing the restrictions of Chapter 90 funds; 
 
WHEREAS, the use of revenue generated through taxation is not restricted for use on public 
ways only; 
 
WHEREAS, a taxation override for the purpose of funding a dedicated Road & Sidewalk Crew, 
allocated $500,000 annually to establish a permanent, in-house DPW repair division specifically 
 
WHEREAS, these override funds are not restricted by the provisions of Chapter 90; 
 
WHEREAS, the City Administration, since 2020, has appropriated $0.00 for the maintenance 
and upkeep of private ways; 
 
WHEREAS, 39% of the streets in the City are private ways, that do not receive their fair share of 
funding for roadway maintenance and upkeep; 
 
WHEREAS, the use of tax revenues for the purpose of maintaining and upgrading our private 
ways is not precluded by state statute; and 
 
WHEREAS, appropriating tax revenues for the purpose of funding for maintenance and upkeep 
of private ways is a budgetary decision of the City Administration; and
4 
 
 
WHEREAS, the City Administration has failed to make equitable delivery of public works 
services a priority; 
 
Be it therefore RESOLVED that the City Administration create and assign a specific account 
and line item for the purpose of funding Private Way Upkeep and Maintenance. 
 
Discussion: 
 
Councilor Scarpelli stated it was important for residents to understand the legalities of what the 
City can and cannot do on private ways, and to understand the process for converting private 
ways to public ways. The City’s Chapter 90 funds may only be used on public ways, and 
because of the large portion of Medford’s roads that are private ways the amount of Chapter 90 
funding the City receives is impacted. Many residents are not aware that they live on a private 
way and are therefore confused when the City notifies them that they are responsible for their 
road. The intent of this paper is therefore to start a dialogue to understand funding and 
responsibilities for private ways and Councilor Scarpelli implored the Mayor and the City’s 
communications team to find an avenue to distribute information about private ways both on 
paper and on the City’s website. Councilor Scarpelli would also like to see a line item 
established in the City’s budget for emergency work on private ways, which could be used to fill 
potholes or remove a tree causing an imminent threat. 
 
President Bears noted that the question of private ways is a perennial concern because of the 
scale of the issue in the City, with the potential cost to the City to adopt all the private ways as 
public ways potentially being as much as $500 million. He stated that the City has been let down 
by decisions made by people 50-100 years ago who laid out the City. Councilor Bears 
recommended that a centralized Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) page be created on the 
City’s website consolidating all of the information on private ways, to which the City can refer 
residents. 
 
Chair Callahan asked whether having a line item in the budget for repairs to private ways could 
pose a legal issue by creating liability for the City. 
 
Commissioner McGivern stated that allocation of specific money for private ways should go 
under Section N in the City’s ordinances for capital projects. However, he is concerned about 
doing that because of the lack of funding for a line item, and he believes the City should wait a 
few years before moving forward with creating a separate line item for private ways. 
 
Commissioner McGivern stated that there are different types of ownership on a private way and 
therefore the City cannot publish a list of private ways, but instead could provide a list of the 
public ways that are under the care and control of the City to assist residents in determining 
whether their property is on a public way. Commissioner McGivern also emphasized the 
importance of residents who are buying a house to investigate the title for the property to 
understand whether it is on a private way. The City is already in the process of drafting a map of 
all of the City’s public ways, and the DPW is also drafting a document providing guidance on the 
responsibility of caring for trees on private ways. The City also does currently work with 
residents on private ways. For example, on Hall Ave, which is a cut-through private way, Todd 
Blake, the City’s Director of Traffic and Transportation, is working with the residents on traffic 
improvements.
5 
 
Commissioner McGivern noted that some private ways would require tens of millions of dollars 
of work to bring them up to the required standards to be adopted as public ways. It is the 
property owners along a private way that pay the cost to bring the way up to public standards so 
that the City can accept it for care and control as a public way. That includes making sure all the 
utilities are installed properly, that there is granite curbing, and that there are sidewalks that are 
the correct width to comply with the ADA. In the 1980s, the City had a poll and levy system 
where there would be a poll of all of the property owners on a private way, and if they were all in 
agreement about the way being adopted as a public way, the City would levy a tax on those 
individual parcels. 
 
Councilor Scarpelli clarified that the line item would be intended to address emergency 
situations but that he understood that the City would need to have a more clearly defined policy 
for use of the funds. He recommended that the Council seek a legal opinion on the liability if the 
City were to establish a line item. Also, in addition to the map of public ways, he requested that 
the website include an explanation of what it means if a street is not listed as a public way. 
 
Motion by Councilor Scarpelli to keep the paper in Committee, to discuss in the Committee 
information that the Council will request to be added to the City’s website regarding private 
ways, and to request guidance from legal counsel on having a line item in the City budget for 
maintenance of private ways. Seconded by President Bears. Approved on a Roll Call Vote of 
Five in favor, Zero opposed. 
 
 
Adjournment: 
 
Motion by Councilor Bears to adjourn, seconded by Councilor Lazzaro. Approved on a Roll Call 
Vote of Four in favor, One opposed (Councilor Leming). 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
Laurel Siegel 
City Clerk
C O M M I T T E E  O N  P U B L I C  W O R K S  A N D  F A C I L I T I E S
Snow Removal on 
Private Ways
What M.G.L. c. 40, § 6C allows, how voters would decide, and what it 
means for the City’s responsibility for private streets
Order 26-172 · Medford City Council · October 21, 2026
B A C K G R O U N D
First, two kinds of streets
Public way
A street the City has formally accepted. The City must 
keep it in repair and clear of snow.
If a defect causes an injury, a person can bring a claim 
against the City, within limits set by state law.
Private way
A street the City has never accepted. Its owners, 
usually the neighbors along it, are responsible for it.
Many private ways are still open to anyone to drive or 
walk on.
39% of Medford’s roadways are private ways, according to 26-172.
Snow Removal on Private Ways · M.G.L. c. 40, § 6C 2
O V E R V I E W
The short version
1 § 6C lets the City spend money to plow private ways. Only Medford voters can adopt it.
2 It covers snow and ice only, not potholes, patching, or other repairs.
3 Plowing under § 6C won’t count as a “repair” that makes the City responsible for the street.
4 Repairs fall under a different law, § 6N. Medford already has a § 6N ordinance, Sec. 74-91, and the Council can 
update it without a ballot vote.
Snow Removal on Private Ways · M.G.L. c. 40, § 6C 3
T H E  L A W
What § 6C does, and doesn’t do
If voters adopt § 6C… Answer
Can the City spend money to clear snow and ice from private ways open to the public? Yes
Does the City Council choose which private ways get plowed? Yes
Is plowing kept from counting as a “repair” of the street? Yes
Does it cover potholes, patching, sweeping, or other repairs? No
Must the City plow every private way? No
Does any private way become a public street, or change owners? No
Source: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6C 4
T H E  L A W
How Medford would adopt § 6C
STEP 1 · NOW
Council puts it on the ballot
This is what Paper 26-172 would do.
STEP 2 · NOV. 2027
Voters decide
If a majority votes yes at the city 
election, § 6C takes effect.
STEP 3 · BEFORE WINTER
Council picks the streets
The Council names which private ways 
get plowed and sets aside funds.
Why a ballot vote?
State law (§ 6D) says a city must ask its voters. The 
Council can’t adopt § 6C on its own. The next regular 
city election is November 2027.
WHAT VOTERS WILL SEE
“Shall the city vote to accept the provisions of section six C of 
chapter forty of the General Laws, which authorize cities and 
towns to appropriate money for the removal of snow and ice from 
private ways therein open to public use?”
Source: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6D 5
W H A T  A  V O T E  W O U L D  M E A N
Today vs. a yes vote vs. a no vote
Today If voters say yes If voters say no
Can the City pay to plow private ways? It plows now, but state guidance 
says it needs § 6C to pay for it
Yes, on streets the Council picks No clear authority; harder to 
justify
Could plowing make the City 
responsible for a street?
Unclear: a court could call it a 
“repair”
No: § 6C says plowing isn’t a 
repair
Unclear, same as today
Do repair rules change? No No No
Does any street become public? No No No
In short: a yes vote puts plowing on solid legal footing; a no vote leaves it uncertain.
State guidance: Division of Local Services letter to Wellfleet, December 2, 2005 6
L I A B I L I T Y
How the City’s liability works today
PUBLIC STREETS
If a defect causes an injury, a person can bring a claim 
against the City.
State law limits these claims: damages are capped at 
$5,000, and the injured person must notify the City 
quickly.
PRIVATE STREETS
Normally, the City isn’t responsible.
But if the City repaired the street in the six years 
before an injury, a court can treat it like a public 
street.
The key point: every repair the City makes on a private way can bring liability with it.
Sources: M.G.L. c. 84, §§ 15, 18, 25 7
L I A B I L I T Y
What a yes vote changes for liability
Protected
Plowing and salting the private ways the Council 
picks. These won’t count as a “repair.”
Not protected
• Filling potholes and patching
• Street sweeping and other upkeep
• Damage from careless plowing, such as to a car or 
fence (a separate law, c. 258, applies)
§ 6C is permission to pay for snow and ice removal,plus one narrow protection. Repairs need a different fix: § 6N.
Sources: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6C; c. 84, § 25; c. 258 8
R E P A I R S
§ 6N: the law for repairing private ways
What it does
It lets a city adopt an ordinance setting the 
rules for temporary repairs on private ways.
No ballot vote is needed. The Council can 
adopt or change the ordinance itself.
The ordinance must decide…
1. What repairs are allowed
2. Whether drainage is included
3. Whether repairs must be a public necessity
4. How many neighbors must ask for repairs
5. Whether neighbors share the cost (betterments)
6. The City’s liability limit for damage from repairs
7. How long the street must have been open to the public
8. Whether a cash deposit is required
Source: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6N 9
R E P A I R S
Medford’s ordinance: Sec. 74-91
What § 6N says to decide What Sec. 74-91 says Status
What repairs are allowed Broad: includes reconstruction and resurfacing Covered
Whether drainage is included Drainage may be included Covered
Public necessity Not addressed; left to the mayor Missing
How many neighbors must ask 51% of neighbors who live on the street Covered
Whether neighbors share the cost Not addressed Missing
City’s liability limit Not addressed Missing: key gap
Years open to the public Five years or more Covered
Cash deposit Not addressed Missing
Sources: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6N; Medford Code Sec. 74-91 (adopted 1986, last amended 2008) 10
R E P A I R S
Updating Sec. 74-91
Why it needs an update
No liability limit: City repairs can still make it 
responsible for a street.
Unused: per the order, $0 has gone to private-way 
repairs since 2020, so patching happens outside it.
Very broad: “temporary” repairs include 
reconstruction and resurfacing.
Possible changes
1. Set a limit on the City’s liability for damage caused by repairs
2. State that repairs don’t make a street public or promise future repairs
3. Have neighbors who request repairs agree to cover related claims
4. Decide on cost-sharing, public necessity, and deposits
5. Add a simple process for small safety fixes, like potholes
The Council can make these changes by ordinance.
Source: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6N 11
N E X T  S T E P S
If voters say yes: what comes next
Choosing streets
The Council names which private ways 
get plowed. Criteria and a street list 
should be ready before the first 
winter.
Which streets qualify
Only ways “open to public use.” 
Streets posted private or used as 
driveways may not qualify.
Funding
§ 6C allows spending but doesn’t 
provide money. The Council would set 
aside funds each year.
For residents: City plowing won’t make your street public, and it isn’t a promise of paving.
Source: M.G.L. c. 40, § 6C 12
Chair Callahan and President Bears, 
 
I look forward to discussing 26-172 and 26-182 about private ways with you and the other 
Councilors later today. I’m in favor of adopting Section 6C, so I’m glad to see that. I want to get a 
few corrections or clarifications on the record in writing, but I can also bring them up later to 
discuss.  
 
It is mentioned that the City has “appropriated $0 for private way repairs”. This is not true. 
Filling potholes is a type of repair, and it is appropriated annually into the Highway operations 
budget. Private ways tend to need a lot of pothole asphalt, so we also occasionally “box out” 
patch areas that do not accept pothole repairs any longer due to pavement degradation.  
 
It is mentioned that the City Admin relies “solely on Chapter 90 funds for the maintenance and 
upkeep of City roads”. We have relied heavily on Chapter 90 for capital projects at the level of 
milling and overlays and other preventative maintenance activities on the public way network. 
This year, the City Council recently appropriated money for $1.3 Million in milling and paving, 
which is more than matching Chapter 90 funding. This type of annual commitment, likely more, 
is needed to maintain or increase our public way network pavement condition index (PCI) over 
time. 
 
It is mentioned that the City Admin has a “policy of refusing to perform certain routine 
maintenance and upkeep of private ways, citing the restrictions of Chapter 90 funds”. We do not 
have such a policy, and the only services we refuse are capital improvements. We are following 
well established Mass General Law, including public obligations to the public way road network. 
We provide minor repairs (potholes), plow and de-icing services, and sweeping. These activities, 
and investments, are all a part of maintenance and upkeep and are provided to private ways in 
Medford. 
 
It is mentioned the “override funds are not restricted by the provisions of Chapter 90”. That is 
true, however, they are restricted to public obligations, including some limited maintenance and 
upkeep of private ways as previously mentioned. The override funds our Highway Operations, 
which covers the municipal public ways and the private ways.  
 
It is mentioned that the “City Administration, since 2020, has appropriated $0 for the 
maintenance and upkeep of private ways.” This is not true. As stated above, we appropriate 
money every year into the Highway budget for limited upkeep and maintenance services which 
are allowed on private ways. 2020 is relevant since we have been tracking our PCI for the public 
way network since that time. That annual assessment helps clearly advise on our obligations to 
the public way road network. 
 
The City has an Ordinance, Temporary repairs of private ways, Section 74-91. It allows frontage 
holders of private ways to petition the City for “temporary repairs” subject to appropriation and 
approval from the Mayor and City Council and recommendation from myself and the City 
Engineer. This is further defined to be activities up to reconstruction. This Ordinance has not
been used since understanding the condition of the public way road network after completing 
our first pavement assessment.  Since the public way road network is an obligation of the City 
and the DPW, we have not been in a position to recommend funds be spent on private ways. 
This will likely be the case until we have a stable PCI at an acceptable level for the public way 
road network. At that future time, we could consider additional funding for private way capital 
improvements. 
 
And lastly, it is good to be aware that there already exists a process to have a private way 
become a public way. Most roads partake in this evolution, but some do not for a variety of 
reasons. The process requires investment in one way or another from the frontage holders of 
the road. In the past, the City has performed proactive poll and levy style conversions/takings of 
private ways, and private way owners are always allowed to improve their own road and 
petition the City for acceptance. It is not cheap, but if you own a parcel on a public road, a 
previous owner of your parcel paid for the improvements either in the initial sale price of their 
home, or later when the road was upgraded when funds became available. Some private ways 
need minimal investment to become public way standard, but others would need to be re-built 
and possibly widened. 
 
I hope this information is helpful for tonight’s discussion. Happy to expand on any of this and 
discuss. 
 
Regards, 
Tim
